nameStory: The name 'bladder-senna' comes from this shrub's most distinctive feature: inflated, papery seed pods that look like tiny balloons or bladders. These puffy pods make a delightful rattling sound when you shake them, filled with loose seeds that dance around inside like nature's own maraca.
description: Bladder-senna is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall with an open, somewhat sprawling habit. Originally from Europe and North Africa, it's grown as an ornamental plant in New England gardens and occasionally escapes to grow wild. The shrub produces clusters of bright yellow pea-like flowers followed by its signature inflated seed pods that look like small green lanterns hanging from the branches.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large, inflated seed pods that look like translucent green balloons or bladders, about 2-3 inches long. When ripe, they become papery and rattle when shaken, containing loose seeds that you can hear moving inside.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow pea-like flowers arranged in small clusters of 3-8 blooms. Each flower has the typical legume shape with a large upper petal and smaller side and bottom petals.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-13 small, oval leaflets arranged along a central stem. The leaflets feel smooth and have a blue-green tint, creating a delicate, feathery appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Open, somewhat loose shrub with arching branches that can look a bit wild or unkempt. Often wider than it is tall, with flexible stems that bend easily in wind.

habitat: In New England, bladder-senna is primarily found in cultivated landscapes, parks, and gardens where it's planted for ornamental purposes or erosion control. It occasionally escapes cultivation and can be found growing wild on disturbed soils, roadsides, and sunny slopes. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun locations.

seasonality.spring: New compound leaves emerge in late spring with their distinctive blue-green color and delicate appearance.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow pea-like flowers bloom from mid to late summer, followed by the development of the characteristic inflated green seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn papery brown, rattling in the wind. Leaves may turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches with persistent brown seed pods that continue to rattle and can help with identification even after leaves have fallen.

funFact: The inflated seed pods act like tiny hot air balloons that can actually help the plant disperse its seeds on the wind, and children have used the dried pods as natural 'poppers' for hundreds of years because they make such a satisfying snap when squeezed!
confusionNotes: The inflated, balloon-like seed pods make this plant nearly impossible to confuse with anything else once you see them. Before the pods form, the yellow pea flowers might be confused with other legumes, but the distinctive blue-green compound leaves help distinguish it.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name containing 'senna,' this plant is not related to true senna plants used medicinally. The name refers only to the similar-looking compound leaves, and bladder-senna should not be used for any medicinal purposes.
compareHints: Bladder-senna is the only species in its genus found in New England. Compared to other leguminous shrubs in the pea family, its inflated seed pods are completely unique - no other shrub in our region produces these balloon-like fruits. Other legume shrubs like black locust have flat pods, and most herbaceous legumes have much smaller, less conspicuous seed pods.
